Welcome! Have you ever wondered where the spark of innovation really starts? It’s often born from uncertainty—when bold ideas collide with the unpredictable twists of the marketplace.
That’s exactly what we’ll explore together as we dive into The Lean Startup, brought to life by Eric Ries. This isn’t just about launching a business—it's about the thrill of turning inspiration into something real and lasting.
What if, instead of clinging to a perfect plan, you could move forward by quickly experimenting, learning from what doesn't work, and adapting on the fly? That’s the power of the Lean Startup approach. It’s a mindset built on agility, listening to customers, and always improving, rather than relying on rigid planning or just hoping things go right.
In this journey, building a startup becomes a living cycle—build, measure, learn, and repeat. Every step brings fresh insights, helping shape your product and your strategy, right as you go. Here, progress means testing your assumptions, making smart use of your resources, and focusing on results that truly matter—not just numbers that look good on paper.
As we travel this path, you’ll notice the shift—from chasing grand plans to taking meaningful, actionable steps. That’s what empowers innovators to face uncertainty head-on, with confidence and resilience.
The real promise of the Lean Startup? It’s about channeling creative energy into something that lasts, opening the door to a whole new era of entrepreneurial success. So, are you ready to explore what it takes to turn an idea into impact? Let’s get started—together.

Chapter 1: Rethinking How New Ventures Begin and Grow
Think about the excitement that comes with starting something new—a business, a product, maybe even a service. There's usually this rush of energy and a bold vision lighting the way forward, right?
But if we're honest, most folks follow the same old playbook: map out a detailed plan, build the entire product behind closed doors, and then cross their fingers, hoping customers will show up.
It feels safe, sure. But more often than not, it leads to wasted effort, missed chances, and sometimes, the whole thing just fizzles out.
Here’s something to really pay attention to—the real reason for a startup isn’t just to make stuff or stick to a plan. It’s to learn how to build something that actually lasts. And this learning? It isn’t about filling your head with theory. It’s about rolling up your sleeves and figuring out, firsthand, what your customers truly want—and how you can deliver it, without burning through all your resources.
Now, whether you’re starting from scratch or working inside a big company, every new venture faces one big challenge: uncertainty. There’s no proven path to follow. You can’t rely on old data or what worked last year.
So, what do you do? You shift your mindset. Instead of just executing a fixed plan, you start running experiments. You test ideas. You look for clues about what actually works.
Picture this: a scientist in a lab, running experiments to see how things react. For startups, the marketplace becomes your lab, and your experiments are the products or features you put out there. And the point isn’t to prove you were right from the beginning—it’s to learn, and to learn fast, what needs to change.
There are a few guiding principles to keep in mind here:
First, startups exist to learn what customers truly want—not just to build things for the sake of building.
Second, progress should be measured by validated learning—that’s real evidence that customers care about what you’re offering.
And third, every step you take should be seen as an experiment, designed to test a specific belief about your business.
Let’s make this real. Imagine a small team working on a brand new mobile app. Instead of spending months perfecting every little detail, they launch a simple version to a handful of users. They watch, carefully, to see which features people actually use—and which ones get ignored.
Every tap, every swipe, tells them something important. They’re not just guessing anymore. They’re learning, directly from the folks who matter most.
And this idea goes way beyond tech startups. You’ll see it in big companies launching new products, nonprofits trying out new programs, even government teams rolling out new services. No matter where you are, the goal is the same: navigate uncertainty by testing ideas quickly, and learning from what happens.
So, instead of measuring success by how many features you’ve built or how much money you’ve raised, focus on the evidence. Are you getting closer to something people will actually pay for and use? That’s what counts.
And that evidence? It comes from real-world experiments—not just meetings or market research.
So, here’s the key takeaway: the Lean Startup mindset is all about learning what works in the real world, as quickly and efficiently as possible. It means questioning your assumptions, getting comfortable with uncertainty, and treating every step as a chance to gather feedback you can use.
If you can embrace that, you’ll be miles ahead on your journey to building something that truly matters.

Chapter 2: The Build-Measure-Learn Feedback Loop—The Engine of Progress
Once you realize that a startup's real mission is validated learning, the next question is simple: how do you actually turn your ideas into real knowledge?
That’s where the Build-Measure-Learn feedback loop comes in. It’s a cycle—simple, but incredibly powerful—that keeps you moving forward, one experiment at a time.
Picture this process like a wheel that spins with every new test you run.
First comes Build. You start with an idea—maybe it’s a feature, a product, or just a rough prototype. The key is to make it real, even if it’s only a basic version.
Next, you Measure. Put what you’ve created in front of actual customers. Watch how they use it, listen to what they say, and collect real data about their choices and their reactions.
Then comes the most important part: Learn. You step back, look at the evidence, and ask yourself—did my assumptions hold up, or do I need to shift gears? This is where you figure out your next move: do you double down, pivot, or try something totally new?
The secret? This isn’t a one-and-done thing. It’s a loop—a continuous, repeating process. Every time you go through the cycle, you get a little closer to figuring out what your customers actually want, and how you can deliver it better.
But here’s something to pay attention to: the best teams don’t try to make things perfect before showing them to the world. Instead, they start small—launching what’s called a minimum viable product, or MVP. An MVP isn’t just a rough draft. It’s a smart, focused experiment designed to test your riskiest assumptions as quickly as possible.
Think about a team building a new online service. Instead of building the whole platform, they might whip up a simple landing page that explains the concept and asks visitors to sign up if they’re interested.
If lots of people sign up? Great—the idea has legs. If almost nobody bites, well, that’s valuable feedback too. It lets the team rethink things before they invest too much time or money.
That’s the real magic of the Build-Measure-Learn loop. It keeps you from getting stuck in your own head, or wasting months building something nobody wants. Every turn of the loop is a chance to sharpen your product, tweak your business model, and move a little closer to building something sustainable.
Want to make the most of this cycle? Here are a few practical tips:
First, always look for your riskiest assumptions—the things that could really sink the whole idea if you’re wrong. Tackle those first.
Next, design experiments that give you feedback fast. The quicker you learn, the quicker you can adapt.
And don’t just track feel-good numbers—use actionable metrics that show how customers actually behave, not just how many people clicked “like” or visited your website.
What’s really exciting is that this loop isn’t just for startups. Anytime you’re facing uncertainty and need to learn fast—whether you’re launching a new product, testing a marketing campaign, or even trying out a new hobby—you can use the Build-Measure-Learn cycle to keep moving forward, cut out wasted effort, and get closer to something that truly matters.

Chapter 3: Minimum Viable Product—Learning with the Least Effort
Let’s dive into a core idea at the heart of the Lean Startup approach—the minimum viable product, or MVP.
Think of the MVP as the smallest, simplest version of your product that lets you start learning from real customers, as quickly and efficiently as possible. The aim isn’t to launch something perfect. It’s about getting your idea out there, collecting feedback, and doing it all with minimal time and resources.
But here’s the thing—building an MVP means you’ve got to shift your mindset. Instead of chasing perfection or adding every feature you can think of, you focus on what’s just good enough to test your most important assumption. Sometimes, that might mean launching with only *one* core feature, or even running things manually behind the scenes just to see if people care.
Imagine you’ve got an idea for a new online marketplace. Instead of spending months building a fancy website, what if you simply connect buyers and sellers through email, or a really basic web form? You’d get a chance to see if there’s real demand, before pouring energy and money into building complex technology.
The MVP serves a few crucial purposes. First, it helps you avoid the trap of building something nobody actually wants. Second, it speeds up your feedback loop, so you learn faster. And third, it helps you save precious resources, by focusing only on what’s absolutely necessary to test your idea.
Now, creating an MVP isn’t about cutting corners or serving up a disappointing experience. It’s about being strategic—figuring out the most important question you need answered, and designing the simplest way to get that answer. That often takes a bit of creativity, and a willingness to let go of features that just aren’t essential right now.
There are a few different flavors of MVP, each with their own strengths. For example, the Concierge MVP is all about manually providing your service to a handful of customers, so you can watch their reactions up close. Then there’s the Wizard of Oz MVP, where everything looks automated on the surface, but you’re actually doing the work by hand behind the scenes. And finally, the Landing Page MVP—that’s where you set up a simple web page to gauge interest in your product or service, before you’ve even built anything substantial.
The secret? Stay focused on learning, not impressing. Every feature, every design decision, even your marketing efforts—ask yourself, “Will this help me get the feedback I need?” If not, it can wait.
Honestly, launching an MVP can feel a little uncomfortable, especially if you’re used to delivering polished, finished products. There’s always that fear of negative feedback, or damaging your brand. But here’s something to remember—the risk of building the wrong product is *much* bigger. By starting small and learning fast, you save yourself from costly mistakes and set up a strong foundation for future growth.
In real-life practice, the MVP is just the beginning. Each experiment you run builds on the last one, getting you closer and closer to something your customers truly love. It takes humility, patience, and a real commitment to learning above all else.

Chapter 4: Validated Learning — Measuring What Matters
So, you've got your MVP up and running, and the Build-Measure-Learn loop is in motion. Now comes the real test: how do you know if what you're learning is actually moving you forward? That’s where validated learning steps in. It’s all about using real evidence to prove you’re making progress—no more guessing or relying on gut feelings.
Validated learning means you’re showing, with hard data, that your team is heading toward a business that’s truly sustainable. It’s not about just shipping features or racking up users. The big question is, are those efforts leading to real results? Think more engaged customers, higher retention, or better revenue—not just bigger numbers.
So, how do you get there? You start by laying out clear hypotheses—your best guesses for what might drive success. Then, you test those ideas with experiments, just like a scientist would. Each experiment gives you a chance to prove or disprove an assumption, using metrics that actually matter.
Let’s say your team thinks a new feature will boost user engagement. Instead of just rolling it out and hoping for the best, you launch it to a small group first. You keep a close eye on the data: do people really engage more, or does nothing change? If there’s no improvement, you’ve just learned something valuable—and you can adjust your approach before investing more time.
Here’s something to watch out for: vanity metrics. These are numbers that might look great on a slide deck—like total downloads, page views, or even social media followers—but they don’t tell you if your business is really growing. They can be tempting, but they often hide the real story and give a false sense of progress.
What you want are actionable metrics. These are the numbers that tie directly to customer behavior and business outcomes. For example:
Activation rate—the percentage of users who actually take a key action, like signing up or making their first purchase.
Retention rate—how many users come back over time.
Referral rate—the percentage of people who recommend you to others.
And revenue per user—the average amount each customer brings in.
By tracking these, you’ll see if your experiments are pushing the business in the right direction. Every cycle through the Build-Measure-Learn loop gives you new insights, helping you decide what to try next.
Validated learning also keeps you honest. It stops you from falling into what’s called “success theater”—celebrating activity instead of real results. It reminds you that the goal isn’t just to stay busy, but to build something people truly value—and are willing to pay for.
To make this work, there’s a simple framework called innovation accounting:
First, establish a baseline. See how your product performs with early adopters.
Next, tune the engine. Run experiments and tweak things to improve the key numbers.
Finally, decide if it’s time to pivot or persevere. If things are moving in the right direction, keep going. If not, it might be time to change course.
This disciplined way of measuring ensures every step you take leads to real learning and improvement. Even when things feel uncertain, you’ll have a clear sense of progress—and a better idea of where to focus your energy next.

Chapter 5: Pivot or Persevere—Making Strategic Decisions
Let’s dive into one of the biggest crossroads any team faces as they build, measure, and learn: should you keep going down your current path, or is it time to make a sharp turn and try something new?
This moment—deciding to pivot or persevere—is absolutely critical for startups and innovation projects alike.
Now, when we talk about a pivot, we’re not talking about giving up. It’s actually a smart, structured move—a course correction based on real evidence. Think of it as testing out a new fundamental idea about your product, your strategy, or even your whole business model.
And here’s something important: pivoting doesn’t mean you’ve failed. It just means you’re responding to what the data is telling you, instead of sticking with something that isn’t working.
There are several different types of pivots, each one aimed at a different part of your business. For example, there’s the zoom-in pivot—that’s when you realize one feature is so valuable, it deserves to become the whole product.
Or maybe it’s the zoom-out pivot, where you see that your original idea is too narrow, and you need to add more features or services to better serve your customers.
Sometimes, you might need a customer segment pivot, which means shifting your focus to a group of customers who are showing more genuine interest.
There’s also the channel pivot, where you change how you deliver or sell your product—maybe to reach people more effectively.
And let’s not forget the technology pivot, which is all about using new technology to provide the same solution, only faster or more efficiently.
So, how do you decide whether to pivot or persevere? The answer is simple: look at your data, not just your gut.
Use the experiments you’ve run and the metrics you’ve tracked to see if you’re actually making progress. If your key numbers are moving in the right direction, and customers are excited, it might be worth sticking with your current approach and refining it.
But if the data says otherwise, it’s probably time to consider a pivot.
Let’s be honest—choosing to pivot isn’t always easy. There’s often a lot of emotional investment in the original idea, and nobody likes to admit something isn’t working.
But here’s what separates successful innovators: the courage to change direction when the evidence calls for it.
One helpful tip? Set up regular “pivot or persevere” meetings with your team. These are structured check-ins, where everyone reviews progress and discusses whether it’s time to make a change. It makes honest reflection part of your rhythm, and keeps you from drifting aimlessly when things aren’t working out.
Remember, perseverance isn’t about stubbornly sticking to your plan no matter what. It’s about continuing to experiment and improve— as long as there are signs of progress.
Pivoting, meanwhile, is about realizing that a new approach might be the best way to reach your ultimate goal.
Both paths take courage, discipline, and a real commitment to learning.
By staying open to change, you can avoid the trap of sunk costs and actually build something that matters.

Let's dive into Chapter 6: Innovation Accounting—Tracking Real Progress.
Now that we've figured out how to experiment and make decisions, the next big question is: How do we know we’re actually getting somewhere?
That’s where innovation accounting steps in. Think of it as your set of signposts on a foggy road. When you can’t quite see the destination, and the path feels uncharted, these markers let you know if you’re headed in the right direction—or if it’s time to rethink your route.
Here’s how the process usually unfolds—there are three main stages.
First, you establish a baseline. This just means you start by measuring how your product is doing with those first, brave users. Are people signing up? Are they coming back? Maybe they’re even telling their friends? The point is to get a clear read on where you stand before any tweaks or changes.
Next, it’s time to tune the engine. You run experiments—maybe you change a feature, adjust the price, or test out a new marketing message. Each test is there to nudge those key numbers up, showing real evidence that your business model is getting stronger.
And then, you come to the crossroads: do you pivot, or do you persevere? You look at the data. If the numbers keep getting better, it might be time to grow. But if things are flat, it’s a signal that you should try something different.
Let’s make this real with an example. Imagine a team launching a subscription service. They start by tracking how many people sign up for a free trial—that’s their baseline. Then, they experiment with different onboarding flows to see if more users become paying subscribers—this is tuning the engine. If, after a few rounds, they still aren’t seeing great conversion rates, they might pivot by changing their target audience or rethinking the pricing.
The heart of innovation accounting is focusing on actionable metrics—numbers that actually reflect what customers are doing and how the business is performing. It’s easy to get distracted by vanity metrics, like total app downloads, but what really matters is how many people are using your app every week.
To keep things simple, teams often use dashboards or spreadsheets to visualize progress over time. The trick is to look for trends and patterns, not just random data points. That way, you can really see if your work is leading to lasting growth or if it’s time to chart a new course.
By bringing innovation accounting into the mix, teams build a culture where everyone’s accountable and decisions are transparent. You cut out the guesswork, and every resource goes toward what actually makes a difference.
So, if you want to know you’re truly making progress, don’t just hope—measure it. That’s the power of innovation accounting.

Chapter 7: Lean Thinking at Scale—Growing Without Losing Agility
So, you’ve built something people really love, and your business model’s clicking. Now, it’s time for that next big leap—scaling up. Sounds exciting, right? But here’s the catch: what helped your tight-knit startup thrive may not work so well once things get bigger.
Lean thinking at scale is all about holding onto that experimental, learning-driven mindset, even as your company grows. Imagine you’re tending a garden. As you add new plants—maybe that’s new teams, new products, or fresh processes—you’ve got to make sure the soil stays rich and supportive, so everything can keep growing strong.
Let’s talk about a few practices that really help keep things agile as you expand.
First, keep your teams small and cross-functional. Small groups move fast and don’t get bogged down by layers of approval. And when you mix in people from engineering, design, marketing, and support, you get a much fuller picture—and better decisions.
Next up: decentralize your decision-making. Let your teams run their own experiments and make changes based on what the data says, not just what the boss thinks. That way, you avoid bottlenecks and stay nimble, even as you grow.
Another big one is to standardize the Build-Measure-Learn loop. Make this feedback cycle a habit for every team. When everyone’s speaking the same language of experiment and learning, it’s much easier to work together—even across a big organization.
Of course, there’s a danger here: getting stuck in “process for process’s sake.” Too many rules or approvals can kill creativity and slow you down. So, instead, aim for lightweight systems that actually help people experiment and learn.
Take this for example—a growing company might set up regular “innovation days,” where teams are encouraged to try out bold new ideas and share what they learn, win or lose. Or, maybe they use a central dashboard where everyone can see each team’s experiments and results, learning from both the hits and the misses.
Culture matters, too. Leaders have to walk the talk by showing curiosity, humility, and a real willingness to learn from failure. When you celebrate experiments—even the ones that don’t pan out—you send a powerful message: learning matters more than always being right.
So, what’s the real secret to scaling with lean thinking? It’s a balancing act—giving just enough structure to support growth, without losing the flexibility to adapt and innovate. If you can pull that off, you’ll build a company that keeps its edge, no matter how big it gets.

Chapter 8: Lean Startup in Established Organizations—Overcoming Barriers
So, what happens when you try to bring the Lean Startup mindset into big companies, nonprofits, or even government agencies?
You might think established organizations have it easier because they've got more resources. But, in reality, they also have something else—lots of built-in resistance and a tendency to stick to the old ways.
Imagine introducing a brand-new species into a thriving ecosystem. If the conditions aren’t just right, it’s probably not going to survive. That’s what it’s like trying to spark innovation inside these larger organizations.
There are some common roadblocks you’ll probably recognize. First up, fear of failure. In a lot of places, making mistakes is seen as a disaster, so people avoid risks altogether. Then there’s bureaucracy and silos. Endless approval chains and rigid departments slow everything down and make creative collaboration tough. And let’s not forget the short-term focus—everyone wants results right now, which makes it hard to invest in experiments that might take time to pay off.
So, how do you break through all that?
Well, one powerful move is to create protected spaces for innovation. Think of “innovation labs” or small, dedicated teams that are free to try new things—even if those things don’t always work out. It’s about giving people the room to experiment without worrying about the consequences.
Another big one is aligning incentives with learning. Instead of just rewarding teams for pulling off successful projects, you celebrate their willingness to run experiments and share what they’ve learned—win or lose. That way, learning becomes part of the culture.
Streamlining processes is key, too. If you can cut down the red tape around approvals and funding, teams can launch experiments quickly and adjust on the fly.
Let’s look at a real-world example. Picture a big retailer that wants to roll out a new digital service. Instead of dragging the idea through the usual layers of approval, they put together a small, cross-functional team, give it its own budget, and let it make decisions. This team dives right into the Build-Measure-Learn loop, testing ideas with real customers and tweaking things based on feedback. If something works, they scale it up. If not, they treat the setback as a lesson learned, not a failure.
And here’s something you can’t overlook—leaders set the tone. When they openly support experimentation and learning, they create a safe space for new ideas to grow. Sometimes, that means challenging old assumptions and rethinking what success looks like.
So, what’s the big picture? It’s about weaving Lean Startup principles into the way an organization operates every day. When continuous learning and adaptation become second nature, that’s when real innovation takes root.

Chapter 9: Continuous Deployment and Adaptation — Building for Change
As organizations grow and mature, being able to change direction quickly becomes more than just helpful—it’s essential. That’s where continuous deployment comes in.
Imagine continuous deployment like a river that never stops flowing. Instead of building up a dam and letting all the water loose at once, this river moves steadily, shifting and adapting whenever it hits a bump in the path. That steady flow? It lets teams respond to customer feedback almost instantly—fixing issues, rolling out new features, and keeping the momentum going.
So, what really makes continuous deployment work? Let’s break down the essentials.
First, there’s automated testing. This means using smart software tools to check for bugs and errors before any new code gets released. Think of it as having a safety net that catches problems early, so you don’t end up releasing something broken. It speeds things up and keeps surprises to a minimum.
Next up, feature flags. Instead of launching new features for everyone all at once, feature flags let you test things out with just a small group of users first. Kind of like giving a sneak peek to a select audience. This way, you can see how things work in a real-world setting, gather honest feedback, and make tweaks before rolling it out to everyone.
And then there’s rapid rollback. If something goes sideways with a new release, you want to be able to quickly hit “undo” and get back to a version that works. It’s all about minimizing headaches for your customers and keeping things running smoothly.
Continuous deployment really shines when it comes to the Build-Measure-Learn loop. Because updates are happening all the time, teams can experiment with new ideas, see how users respond, and learn from the results—sometimes in just a day or two. It turns the whole process into a fast-paced conversation between your product and your users.
This mindset also helps foster a culture of constant improvement. Instead of waiting around for a huge product launch, teams are always on the lookout for small tweaks and upgrades. Over time, these little changes add up, leading to better quality and happier customers.
Now, embracing continuous deployment does mean making some investments—both in your tools and the way your team works. And sure, it might feel a bit uncomfortable at first, especially if you’re used to long, drawn-out development cycles.
But here’s the big takeaway: the payoff is worth it. You gain agility, you learn faster, and your organization becomes more resilient to change. That’s what makes continuous deployment such a game-changer for any team that’s serious about innovation.

Let’s dive into Chapter 10: The Human Side of Lean—Leadership, Culture, and Mindset.
At its heart, Lean Startup isn’t just about tools or step-by-step processes. It’s really about a mindset—a way of thinking that values learning, humility, and being able to adapt quickly. And that mindset, well, it needs to be nurtured at every level, whether you’re the newest person on the team or leading the whole organization.
Now, when you think about leadership in a Lean environment, it’s not about barking orders or micromanaging every move. Instead, leaders act more like gardeners. They create the right environment, clear away obstacles, and give new ideas the space to take root and flourish. Imagine a manager who encourages curiosity, celebrates experiments—even the ones that don’t go as planned—and stands by their team as they navigate all the ups and downs. That’s the kind of leadership that helps innovation thrive.
There are a few simple but powerful principles that help build this kind of culture:
First, embrace uncertainty. Not every idea’s going to work—and that’s okay. Failure isn’t the end; it’s just part of learning.
Second, encourage open communication. Give people a safe space to speak up, share ideas, ask questions, and even challenge the status quo, all without worrying about being judged.
And third, model humility. The best leaders are the ones who admit they don’t have all the answers and are willing to learn right alongside their teams.
Building this kind of Lean culture doesn’t happen overnight. It takes time, effort, and a willingness to let go of old habits. For organizations that have been doing things a certain way for years, this shift can feel pretty challenging. So, how do you get started?
One practical way is to start small. Try out Lean Startup methods with just one team or project. See how it goes, and use those results to inspire others and build momentum for bigger change. As more people experience the benefits of quick learning and being able to adapt, you’ll notice the culture slowly starting to shift.
So, here’s the key takeaway: The human side of Lean is really about creating an environment where people feel safe to take risks, learn from their mistakes, and chase bold ideas. When you get that right, innovation isn’t just something you do—it becomes part of who you are.

As we wrap up, let’s bring it all together. The Lean Startup approach is really about turning the unknown into opportunity—step by step. Instead of relying on rigid plans, you focus on learning, experimenting, and adapting, so you can build products and businesses that actually make a difference for real people—without wasting time and energy on what doesn’t matter.
So, what does this mean for you?
First, start with learning—not just planning. Every step? Treat it like an experiment.
Use the Build-Measure-Learn loop to keep improving, one iteration at a time.
Launch a minimum viable product and test your assumptions out in the real world—fast and efficiently.
Don’t get distracted by flashy numbers; focus on metrics that really tell you what’s working.
When the data says it’s time to change course, don’t be afraid to pivot—or, if you’re on the right track, go all in.
As your idea grows, keep your team agile and make Lean thinking part of your everyday culture.
In bigger organizations, help innovation thrive by breaking down barriers to quick experiments.
And if you can, embrace continuous deployment, so you’re always ready to adapt to customer needs.
Most of all, nurture a spirit of humility, curiosity, and honest communication.
Remember, innovation rarely follows a straight path. There’ll be setbacks, surprises, and moments where you question it all. But if you treat every challenge as a chance to learn, you’ll build not just better products—but a stronger, wiser team.
The Lean Startup method isn’t a magic formula for guaranteed success. It’s a way to stack the odds in your favor by making every step count. So, trust the process, stay open to change, and let real feedback guide your next move.
In the end, your greatest achievement might not be a product or a business—it could be a team and a mindset ready to thrive, no matter what the future brings.
